The bandura is a Ukrainian plucked folk instrument, a chordophone by family, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5 / 314.122. Its construction combines elements of the zither and the lute: early forms looked like a lute, later ones have a stopped fingerboard and extra treble strings on the soundboard (prystrunky), and instruments played today can have as many as 68 strings. The traditional players were mostly blind and were called kobzar; they accompanied their own singing on the bandura, with a repertory of folk songs, psalms, epics and dance tunes, and the instrument also appears at court, in conservatories and in street performance.
班杜拉琴為烏克蘭撥弦樂器，詞彙見於1441年波蘭編年史。其前身可追溯至591年拜: The bandura is a Ukrainian plucked instrument; the word appears in a Polish chronicle of 1441. Its predecessor can be traced to a lute-type instrument recorded in a Byzantine text of 591, and there is an image of one in an eleventh-century fresco in Saint Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv. Zither-like strings were added in the mid-eighteenth century, and in the mid-nineteenth the zither form replaced the lute form; in the twentieth century the number of strings rose to 31, then 56 to 68. It was once popular in the courts of Eastern European nobility; in 1876 a Russian ban suppressed stage playing, after the Kharkiv conference of 1902 it was revived, in 1908 a class opened at the Kyiv conservatory, in 1909 a tutor was published, and in 1910 the first composition for it appeared.
班杜拉琴的音箱主要採用優質木材製成，背板與面板通常使用雲杉或松木，以獲得良好的共: The soundbox of the bandura is mainly of good timber, the back and top usually of spruce or pine, which resonate well. The neck is mostly maple or oak, strong and stable. The strings were historically of gut or horsehair, and modern instruments mostly use nylon or steel. Inside the soundbox are wooden posts and beams for strength, and on top a wooden bridge supports the strings, keeping the tone clear.
班杜拉琴的音色溫潤而富有詩意，兼具明亮與深邃的雙重特質。其高音區清澈透亮，具有琵: The bandura's timbre is warm and poetic, both bright and deep at once. Its high register is clear and transparent, with the penetration of the pipa, while the middle and low register is warm and full, showing the resonance of the dulcimer. With the number of strings raised to 68 its range is much extended, from a deep fundamental to high overtones, in rich layers. It resonates in its own way, the wooden soundbox producing warm harmonics, and when plucked the notes run on naturally into one another, making a continuous, gentle sound. Beside the clear transparency of the Western harp the bandura is warmer and more intimate; beside the pipa its timbre is softer and more delicate. This tone, particular to a folk instrument, is a perfect reading of the lyrical character of Ukrainian music.
